# Spike S1 — Glass and readability over a live screencast

**Feature**: FEAT-069 TASK-001 · **Plan**: `.spec-lite/plan_ui.md` §8 (S1), §10, §14
**Harness**: `e2e/spikes/live-view-s1/` (`run-spike.ts`, `viewer.html`, `metrics.ts`)
**Verdict**: **GO.** The §6 design holds, so no architecture change is needed. See [Decision](#decision).

## Method

- A **source** headless Chrome loads a fixture page with continuous motion: an animated gradient
  hero, three rotating blocks, a 20 Hz text ticker, and 2,600 words of dense five-column serif text.
  The page uses a 1600×1000 viewport, and the source streams it with CDP `Page.startScreencast`
  (JPEG).
- The harness relays frames over a local WebSocket using the §6 delivery model. There is **one
  frame slot (latest wins)** and **one frame in flight** per viewer until the viewer acks it.
- A **viewer** headless Chrome (a separate browser process) decodes each frame with
  `createImageBitmap` and draws it on a `<canvas>` under **four glass panels**. The panels use the
  shipped FEAT-061 values: the tint at the computed scrim floor (`--glass-alpha` 0.775 light / 0.800
  dark), `blur(20px) saturate(1.5)`, and the edge and shadow. FEAT-061 has landed, so no draft CSS
  was needed. The `solid` rows use the opaque Solid-mode panel.
- Each combination ran for **30 s** after a 3 s warm-up. The harness recorded:
  - frame-interval p50 and p95 from the viewer's draw timestamps;
  - main-thread share (`TaskDuration` delta ÷ wall time, from `Performance.getMetrics`) on both
    the viewer and the source target;
  - JPEG bytes;
  - analytic contrast of glass text over pure black and pure white (the FEAT-061 formula, with no
    sampling).

Every glass text token stays at or above 4.5:1 over both extremes, whatever pixels the screencast
puts behind it. (The FEAT-061 token suite proves the same floor with noise included.)

## Findings

1. **Rates are met with a wide margin.** Every combination drew its target rate (5.0 or 10.0 fps)
   with p95 intervals within about 20 ms of the target interval. The viewer main thread stayed
   between 2.8 % and 4.3 % of one core, against the §10 budget of 15 %.
2. **Glass costs almost nothing on the main thread.** Glass and Solid rows at the same settings
   match to within 0.1 percentage point. Backdrop blur runs in the compositor and raster threads,
   which `TaskDuration` does not count. The §10 budget names the main thread, so that is the metric
   TASK-011 enforces. A low-end GPU may still struggle with compositing, and that shows up as a low
   drawn rate, which TASK-011 measures as well.
3. **The §6 frame queue holds 5 and 10 fps.** No frame was replaced in the one-slot queue. The
   viewer always acked before the next capture arrived, so latest-wins delivery with one frame in
   flight adds no visible latency.
4. **Ack pacing must be scheduled serially (input for TASK-006).** Chrome keeps about two
   screencast frames in flight. The first implementation paced each ack from the last ack it had
   sent. Both in-flight frames were then acked together, and Chrome drew **27 fps at a 10 fps
   target**. The fix schedules each ack one interval after the previous _scheduled_ ack
   (`nextAckAt = max(now, nextAckAt + interval)`), which held exactly 5.0 and 10.0 fps.
   `ScreencastSource` must use that rule.
5. **Source cost is flat at about 6 % of one core,** independent of rate and size. Encoding happens
   in the browser process and GPU, not on the page's main thread, so the screencast does not slow
   the run's page work.
6. **Frame size is driven by dense text.** Dense text pushes frames to 188–415 KiB. The default
   (below) is about 250 KiB × 10 fps ≈ 2.5 MB/s over loopback, well under the 4 MiB per-frame cap.

### Caveats

- The viewer was **headless Chrome**, not the `--app` window. Main-thread work (WebSocket, decode
  dispatch, `drawImage`, rAF) is the same. Compositing a visible window costs GPU time that is not
  measured here, and TASK-012's performance case measures it in the real app.
- This harness measures delivery and cost. Readability of _page_ text inside the frames is a
  quality choice, not a budget. It was checked by eye on one captured frame per quality: dense 13 px
  serif text on a 1600×1000 page, scaled to 1280×800, then magnified 2.5×. At q50 the glyphs are
  visibly blockier and words are hard to read. At q70 the words stay readable.

## Decision

- **Go.** Glass over a live screencast meets the §10 budget at both target rates. Solid is still
  required as the automatic fallback (TASK-011) for machines where it does not.
- **No DEVIATION.** The §6 frame-queue design holds 5 fps and more.

### Chosen defaults (TASK-002 / TASK-006)

| Setting                   | Value                                    | Why                                                                    |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Target frame rate         | **10 fps**                               | Twice the §14 floor at about 4 % of one core; leaves headroom to drop  |
| JPEG quality              | **70**                                   | Small text stays readable; q50 is visibly blockier on dense serif text |
| Max size (`frames.start`) | **1280×800**                             | The protocol default; about 250 KiB per frame                          |
| `everyNthFrame`           | **1**                                    | Ack pacing, not frame skipping, sets the rate (finding 4)              |
| Ack pacing                | serial schedule, `interval = 1000 / fps` | Finding 4                                                              |

### Automatic-Solid thresholds (TASK-011)

The plan §10 starting points stand. Measured headroom gives no reason to tighten them:

- **Drawn rate below 5 fps** for two consecutive 5 s windows while the worker offers at least 5
  fps; **or**
- **Live-view main-thread time above 15 % of one core** for two consecutive 5 s windows.

## Linux numbers

**Waived by the user (2026-11-17).** The go decision, defaults and thresholds rest on the Windows
measurements above. A Linux run was planned through a temporary CI workflow, but the repository's CI
cannot install dependencies (`pnpm-lock.yaml` is gitignored), and the user chose not to wait for it.
The workflow has been removed. The automatic-Solid monitor (TASK-011) is the safety net for any
machine, Linux included, where glass over the live view runs over budget.

## Reproduce

```sh
pnpm exec turbo run build --filter=@yantra/ui --filter=@yantra/core
cd e2e
npx tsx spikes/live-view-s1/run-spike.ts --duration 30 --out results.json   # all 10 combinations
npx tsx spikes/live-view-s1/run-spike.ts --duration 5 --only solid          # quick check
npx vitest run spikes/live-view-s1/metrics.spec.ts                          # metrics unit tests
```
